title: Social Studies Practices: Maps, Data, Sources, and Bias
objectives: Students will read maps presented as grids or tables, using direction, a key, and a scale to locate places and measure distance.
Students will interpret bar graphs, line graphs, and tables and choose conclusions that the data actually support.
Students will distinguish primary sources from secondary sources and explain the strengths and limits of each.
Students will identify bias, propaganda techniques, fact versus opinion, and point of view in documents, posters, and cartoons described in words.
Students will identify cause-and-effect relationships and avoid treating a sequence or correlation as proof of cause.
teach:
Objectives

  • Read maps presented as grids and tables, using direction, a key, and a scale.
  • Read bar graphs, line graphs, and tables, and decide which conclusions the data actually support.
  • Tell primary sources from secondary sources and explain what each kind is good for.
  • Recognize bias, propaganda techniques, fact versus opinion, and point of view in documents, posters, and cartoons.
  • Identify cause-and-effect relationships and avoid confusing “happened after” with “was caused by.”

Materials

  • Student Lesson (printed or on screen), including the Pine Valley grid map and the U.S. population table
  • Study sheet (Notes) for each student
  • Whiteboard or shared screen; highlighters in two colors (one for facts, one for opinions)
  • Week 9 Social Studies practice set (12 items)

60-Minute Plan

SegmentMinutesWhat happens
Warm-up5“Fact or opinion?” quick sort and one source question
Direct instruction20Maps; charts and graphs; primary and secondary sources; bias and propaganda; fact, opinion, point of view; cause and effect; worked examples
Guided practice15Four questions worked together
Independent practice15Practice set items 1–8 (finish 9–12 at home)
Wrap-up5Checks for understanding and the exit ticket from the Post Lesson

Warm-up (5 minutes)

Write these four statements on the board and ask students to label each one F (fact) or O (opinion). Then ask the source question.

  1. “The Declaration of Independence was approved on July 4, 1776.” Answer: Fact. It can be checked in historical records.
  2. “The Declaration of Independence is the most beautiful document ever written.” Answer: Opinion. “Most beautiful” is a judgment; people can reasonably disagree.
  3. “The 2020 Census counted about 331 million people in the United States.” Answer: Fact. The Census Bureau's official count was 331,449,281.
  4. “Our town should build a new park instead of a parking garage.” Answer: Opinion. “Should” signals a recommendation.
  5. Source question: “Your grandmother's diary from 1969 and a website article about 1969 written last year: which one was created by someone who lived through the events?” Answer: the diary. That makes it a primary source.

Direct Instruction (20 minutes)

A. Why this week matters (1 minute)

  • The GED Social Studies test is built around documents, maps, charts, cartoons, and short readings. Almost every question gives students something to read or look at first.
  • These practices (reading data, judging sources, separating fact from opinion) are tested no matter what the topic is. A student who masters them can answer questions on topics he or she has never studied.

B. Reading maps (4 minutes)

  • On the test and in this course, some maps are described in words or shown as a grid table. Teach students to find four things first: the title, the orientation (which way is north), the key (what the symbols or labels mean), and the scale (how distance on the map compares to real distance).
  • Directions: north, south, east, west, and the in-between directions northeast, northwest, southeast, southwest. When north is at the top, east is to the right.
  • Grid maps use rows and columns, like a spreadsheet. To find a direction between two places, compare rows first (north or south), then columns (east or west), and combine them.
  • Scale: count squares between two places and multiply by the distance each square represents.

Worked example 1 (grid map). Use the Pine Valley map in the Student Lesson. North is at the top, columns 1–4 run west to east, and each square is 2 miles on a side. The town of Pine Valley is in square A2. Dunmore is in square C4. Lake Ross is in square A4.

Question 1: In which direction is Dunmore from Pine Valley?
Step 1: Rows. Pine Valley is in row A; Dunmore is in row C, two rows lower. Lower on the map means south.
Step 2: Columns. Pine Valley is in column 2; Dunmore is in column 4. A higher column number means east.
Step 3: Combine: south + east = southeast.

Question 2: About how far is Lake Ross from Pine Valley, measured center to center?
Both are in row A. From column 2 to column 4 is 2 squares. 2 squares × 2 miles = 4 miles.

C. Charts, graphs, and tables (4 minutes)

  • Read the title, the axis labels, and the units before reading any numbers. Ask: “What is being measured, in what units, and over what time or for what group?”
  • Bar graphs compare amounts across categories. Line graphs show change over time. Tables give exact values.
  • Know the difference between a percent (a share of a whole) and a count (a number of people or things). A rising percent does not prove that the count rose.
  • A supported conclusion uses only what the data show. Watch for answer choices that go beyond the data, especially ones that claim a cause.

Worked example 2 (table). Use the U.S. population table in the Student Lesson (official census counts, rounded): 1900, 76.2 million; 1950, 151.3 million; 2000, 281.4 million; 2020, 331.4 million.

Which conclusion is supported? (a) The population roughly doubled from 1900 to 1950. (b) Large families caused most of the growth after 1950.

Check (a): 76.2 × 2 = 152.4, and the 1950 count is 151.3, very close. Supported.
Check (b): The table shows only totals. It says nothing about why the population grew. Not supported.
Answer: (a). Point out that (b) may or may not be true; the issue is that this table cannot prove it.

D. Primary and secondary sources (3 minutes)

  • A primary source was created by someone who took part in or witnessed an event, at or near the time: letters, diaries, speeches, laws, photographs, posters, official records, original data.
  • A secondary source describes, explains, or interprets events after the fact, usually using primary sources: textbooks, encyclopedias, documentaries, most history books.
  • Neither type is automatically more accurate. A primary source gives first-hand evidence and shows how people thought at the time, but it reflects the creator's point of view. A secondary source can offer a broader view, but it reflects the author's interpretation.

Worked example 3 (source type). President Abraham Lincoln delivered the Gettysburg Address on November 19, 1863, at the dedication of a national cemetery for soldiers in Gettysburg, Pennsylvania. It begins: “Four score and seven years ago our fathers brought forth on this continent, a new nation, conceived in Liberty, and dedicated to the proposition that all men are created equal.”

Is the speech a primary or secondary source about the Civil War? Primary: Lincoln was a participant, and he gave the speech during the war. Is a 2015 book that analyzes the speech primary or secondary? Secondary: it was written long afterward by someone interpreting the speech.

Follow-up: “Four score and seven” means 4 × 20 + 7 = 87 years. 1863 − 87 = 1776, so Lincoln is pointing back to the Declaration of Independence and its claim that “all men are created equal.”

E. Bias and propaganda (4 minutes)

  • Bias is a one-sided presentation that favors one view. Clues: loaded words (“reckless,” “heroic”), facts left out, only one side quoted, a creator who gains from the reader agreeing.
  • Propaganda is information, often one-sided, spread on purpose to shape public opinion. Governments, groups, and businesses have all used it. Wartime posters are classic GED examples.
  • Teach these common techniques: bandwagon (everyone is doing it), name-calling (attaching a negative label), glittering generalities (vague, feel-good words like “freedom” with no specifics), testimonial (a famous or respected person endorses it), transfer (linking a cause to a respected symbol such as the flag), card stacking (showing only the facts that help one side), plain folks (“I'm just like you”), and fear (warning of danger unless you act).

Worked example 4 (poster described in words). A 1917 U.S. Army recruiting poster by the artist James Montgomery Flagg shows Uncle Sam, a symbol of the United States, wearing a top hat decorated with stars. He looks straight at the viewer and points his finger outward. Large letters read “I WANT YOU FOR U.S. ARMY,” and smaller letters below direct readers to the nearest recruiting station. More than four million copies were printed in 1917 and 1918, during World War I.

Purpose: to persuade men to enlist. Technique: transfer (the respect people feel for their nation is linked to joining the army) plus a direct personal appeal (“YOU”). What the poster is good evidence of: how the government tried to build support for the war. What it is not good evidence of: how many men actually enlisted or how the public really felt.

F. Fact, opinion, and point of view (2 minutes)

  • A fact can be proven true or false with evidence. An opinion is a belief or judgment. Signal words for opinion: should, best, worst, most important, unfair, wise, I believe.
  • Point of view is the position from which a person sees an event. A factory owner and a striking worker can describe the same strike very differently, and both accounts can still be primary sources.

G. Cause and effect (2 minutes)

  • A cause makes something happen; an effect is the result. Signal words: because, as a result, led to, therefore, consequently, due to.
  • Effects often become causes of new events, forming a chain.
  • Warn students: just because B happened after A does not mean A caused B. Two things changing together (correlation) is not proof that one caused the other.

Guided Practice (15 minutes)

Work these together. Have students point to the evidence before answering.

  1. A grid map shows Fairview in square B1 and Kent in square B4. Each square is 10 miles. How far apart are the towns, center to center? Answer: 3 squares × 10 miles = 30 miles. Kent is east of Fairview.
  2. A line graph shows a county's unemployment rate fell from 8% in 2012 to 4% in 2018. A new factory opened in 2014. A student says, “The factory cut unemployment in half.” Is that conclusion supported? Answer: Not by the graph alone. The rate did fall by half, but the graph does not show why. Other causes (a national recovery, people leaving the workforce) could explain the drop. To test the claim, compare counties without a new factory or count how many local people the factory hired.
  3. Label each source primary or secondary: a soldier's 1944 letter home; a 1995 documentary about D-Day; the text of the Nineteenth Amendment; a biography of Susan B. Anthony written in 2005. Answer: primary, secondary, primary, secondary.
  4. “The new highway, which opened in 2021, is a disgraceful waste of money, and only a fool would drive on it.” Identify the propaganda technique and one opinion phrase. Answer: name-calling (“only a fool”); opinion phrase: “disgraceful waste of money.” The fact in the sentence is that the highway opened in 2021.

Checks for Understanding

  • “What four things do you look for first on any map?” Expected: title, orientation (north), key, scale.
  • “Why can't a chart of percents tell you whether the number of people went up?” Expected: a percent is a share of a total; if the total changed, the count could go up or down.
  • “Is a primary source always more trustworthy than a secondary source?” Expected: No. Primary sources reflect the creator's point of view and may be biased or mistaken.
  • “Give one signal word for opinion and one for cause and effect.” Expected: should, best, unfair (opinion); because, led to, as a result (cause and effect).

Common Mistakes and How to Correct Them

Reversing a direction. Students answer “Where is A from B?” by describing where B is from A. Correction: say it aloud as “Start at B. Which way do I travel to reach A?”

Treating a percent as a count. Students read “transit use rose from 11% to 13%” as “more people rode transit.” Correction: ask “13% of how many?” If the chart does not give the total, the count is unknown.

Choosing a cause the data cannot prove. Answer choices with “caused,” “because of,” or “led to” are often traps on data questions. Correction: ask “Does the chart show why, or only what?”

Assuming primary means true. Correction: remind students that a poster, a speech, or a company statement was made to persuade someone. Ask “Who made this, and what did they want?”

Calling any sentence with a number a fact. “The $42,000 cost is far too high” contains a number but is an opinion. Correction: underline the judgment words.

Differentiation

Support: Give students a four-question card for every stimulus: Who made it? When? Why? What does it actually show? For maps, let students draw arrows on the grid. For fact versus opinion, have them highlight judgment words before deciding.

Stretch: Have students find a modern public-service poster or advertisement and name its technique, its audience, and what it leaves out. Or give them the population table and ask them to write one supported conclusion and one tempting but unsupported conclusion, then trade with a partner.

How This Shows Up on the GED

  • Typical wording: “Which conclusion is supported by the data?”, “Which statement is an opinion?”, “What was the purpose of the poster?”, “Which source would be most useful for…?”, “Which information would best help evaluate the claim?”, “Which statement best explains why the two accounts differ?”
  • Formats: multiple choice; drop-down statements; drag-and-drop sorting (for example, primary versus secondary); clicking a sentence in a passage; short numeric answers from a chart or map.
  • Remind students that these skills appear across civics, history, economics, and geography questions, and that this week's Practice GED will test them on many different topics.
student:
Why This Matters

On the GED Social Studies test, almost every question starts with something to read or look at: a map, a graph, a speech, a poster, or a short article. The test is less about memorizing facts and more about using what is in front of you. This week you will practice the skills that work on every topic.

1. Reading Maps

Before you answer any map question, find four things:

Title (what place, what topic) • North (usually the top) • Key (what the labels or symbols mean) • Scale (how far one unit on the map is in real life)

Some maps are shown as a grid. Rows are labeled with letters and columns with numbers. In the map below, north is at the top, so row A is the farthest north and column 4 is the farthest east. Each square is 2 miles on a side.

Pine Valley (fictional)Column 1 (west)Column 2Column 3Column 4 (east)
Row A (north)ForestTown of Pine ValleyFarmlandLake Ross
Row BForestHighway 5Town of Oak SpringsFarmland
Row C (south)QuarryFarmlandFarmlandTown of Dunmore

Worked example 1. In which direction is Dunmore from Pine Valley?

Step 1: Start at Pine Valley (A2). Dunmore is in row C, which is farther down the map: south.
Step 2: Dunmore is in column 4, which is to the right: east.
Step 3: Combine them: southeast.

How far is Lake Ross (A4) from Pine Valley (A2)? Two squares × 2 miles = 4 miles.

2. Reading Charts, Graphs, and Tables

Read the title, the labels, and the units first. Then ask: What exactly is being measured? A bar graph compares groups. A line graph shows change over time. A table gives exact numbers.

YearU.S. population (official census count, rounded)
190076.2 million
1950151.3 million
2000281.4 million
2020331.4 million

Worked example 2. Which conclusion does the table support?
(a) The population roughly doubled between 1900 and 1950.
(b) Large families caused the growth after 1950.

Check (a): 76.2 × 2 = 152.4. The 1950 count, 151.3 million, is very close to that. Supported.
Check (b): The table shows totals only. It never says why the population grew. Not supported.

A percent is a share of a whole, not a number of people. If a graph shows that the share of workers who ride the bus rose from 11% to 13%, you cannot tell whether more people ride the bus unless you also know the total number of workers.

3. Primary and Secondary Sources

Primary sourceSecondary source
Who made it?Someone who took part in or saw the eventSomeone who studied the event later
When?At or near the timeAfter the fact
ExamplesLetters, diaries, speeches, laws, photographs, posters, original recordsTextbooks, encyclopedias, documentaries, most history books
StrengthFirst-hand evidence; shows how people thought thenBroader view; puts events in context
CautionShows only the creator's point of viewShows the author's interpretation

Worked example 3. On November 19, 1863, during the Civil War, President Abraham Lincoln spoke at the dedication of a soldiers' cemetery in Gettysburg, Pennsylvania. His speech begins: “Four score and seven years ago our fathers brought forth on this continent, a new nation, conceived in Liberty, and dedicated to the proposition that all men are created equal.”

The speech is a primary source: Lincoln was a leader in the war, and he spoke while it was happening. A modern article explaining the speech would be a secondary source.

Bonus: a “score” is 20. Four score and seven = 4 × 20 + 7 = 87. 1863 − 87 = 1776, the year of the Declaration of Independence.

4. Bias and Propaganda

Bias means presenting only one side. Look for loaded words, missing facts, and a creator who benefits if you agree. Propaganda is one-sided information spread on purpose to shape what the public thinks or does. Common techniques:

  • Bandwagon: “Everyone is joining. Don't be left out.”
  • Name-calling: attaching a negative label to a person or idea.
  • Glittering generalities: vague, positive words (“freedom,” “progress”) with no details.
  • Testimonial: a famous or trusted person endorses the idea.
  • Transfer: linking an idea to a respected symbol, such as the flag.
  • Card stacking: showing only the facts that help one side.
  • Fear: warning of danger unless you act.

Posters and political cartoons are usually described in words on this course's tests. Read the description slowly: notice who or what is shown, any labels, and any words printed on the image. Then ask, “What does the creator want me to think or do?”

5. Fact, Opinion, and Point of View

A fact can be checked and proven true or false. An opinion is a belief or judgment. Watch for opinion words: should, best, worst, unfair, wonderful, I believe.

Worked example 4. “The city council voted 5 to 2 to raise bus fares to $2.00. The increase is unfair to working families.”

Sentence 1 is a fact: the vote and the new fare can be checked in council records. Sentence 2 is an opinion: “unfair” is a judgment.

Point of view is the position a person sees from. A mill owner and a mill worker may describe the same strike in completely different ways. Both accounts are primary sources, and each tells you something true about how that person saw events.

6. Cause and Effect

A cause is why something happens; an effect is what happens as a result. Signal words: because, led to, as a result, therefore, due to. Effects often become causes of new events, creating a chain.

Just because one thing happened after another does not mean the first thing caused it. On data questions, be suspicious of any answer that says “caused” unless the evidence clearly shows the cause.

Try It

1. Using the Pine Valley map, in which direction is Pine Valley from Dunmore?

Show answer

Northwest. Start at Dunmore (C4). Pine Valley is in row A (north) and column 2 (west).

2. Using the population table, by how many millions did the U.S. population increase from 2000 to 2020?

Show answer

331.4 − 281.4 = 50.0 million.

3. Primary or secondary? (a) A photograph taken at a 1963 civil rights march. (b) An encyclopedia article about the causes of World War I.

Show answer

(a) Primary: it was made at the event. (b) Secondary: it explains events after the fact.

4. A poster shows a famous baseball player saying, “I buy savings bonds. You should too!” Which propaganda technique is this?

Show answer

Testimonial: a well-known person endorses the action.

5. Fact or opinion? “The new library hours are the best decision the county has ever made.”

Show answer

Opinion. “The best decision” is a judgment that cannot be proven.
post:
Summary of Key Points

  • On any map, find the title, north, the key, and the scale first. For direction, start at the place named second (“from ___”) and ask which way you travel.
  • On any chart, read the title, labels, and units first. A percent is a share, not a count. A supported conclusion uses only what the data show.
  • Primary sources come from people who were there at the time; secondary sources interpret events afterward. Neither is automatically more accurate.
  • Bias and propaganda present one side to shape opinion. Common techniques include bandwagon, name-calling, glittering generalities, testimonial, transfer, card stacking, and fear.
  • Facts can be checked; opinions are judgments. Point of view shapes what a writer notices and how he or she describes it.
  • “Happened after” is not the same as “was caused by.”

Exit Ticket

1. On a grid map with north at the top, Town X is in square D1 and Town Y is in square A1. In which direction is Town Y from Town X?

Show answer

North. Row A is above row D, and both towns are in column 1.

2. Is a diary kept by a nurse during World War II a primary or secondary source?

Show answer

Primary. The nurse lived through the events and wrote at the time.

3. “Join the millions of Americans who have already signed up!” Which propaganda technique is this?

Show answer

Bandwagon.

4. Fact or opinion? “The Nineteenth Amendment was ratified in 1920.”

Show answer

Fact. It can be checked in official records.

5. A town's crime rate fell the year after it installed brighter streetlights. Does that prove the lights caused the drop? Explain in one sentence.

Show answer

No. The drop came after the lights, but other things (more police patrols, a change in the economy) could explain it; you would need more evidence, such as comparing similar towns without new lights.

Reflection

  • Which skill from this week feels strongest for you, and which one do you want to practice more?
  • Think of an advertisement or social media post you saw recently. Which technique did it use, and what did it leave out?
  • Why might two honest people who witnessed the same event write very different accounts of it?

Test-Taking Strategy: Read the Stimulus Like a Detective

Before reading the question, spend 20 seconds on the stimulus: read the title, the source line, the labels, and the units. Ask “Who made this, when, and why?” Then read the question. When you check the answer choices, cross out any choice that claims more than the stimulus shows, especially choices with words like “caused,” “always,” or “proves.”

vocab.def: A record created by someone who took part in or witnessed an event, at or near the time it happened.
vocab.example: A letter a soldier wrote home in 1863.

vocab.def: A work that describes or interprets events after they happened, usually based on primary sources.
vocab.example: A textbook chapter about the Civil War.

vocab.def: A one-sided view that favors one position and leaves out or downplays others.
vocab.example: An article about a strike that quotes only the factory owner.

vocab.def: Information, often one-sided, spread on purpose to shape public opinion or behavior.
vocab.example: A wartime poster urging people to enlist.

vocab.def: A statement that can be proven true or false with evidence.
vocab.example: The 2020 Census counted about 331 million people in the United States.

vocab.def: A statement of belief, feeling, or judgment that cannot be proven true or false.
vocab.example: “The new bridge is the ugliest building in town.”

vocab.def: The position or perspective from which a person sees and describes events.
vocab.example: A worker and an owner describe the same strike differently.

vocab.def: A relationship in which one event (the cause) makes another event (the effect) happen.
vocab.example: A long drought led to crop failures.

vocab.def: Two things that change at the same time or in a pattern; this alone does not prove that one causes the other.
vocab.example: Ice cream sales and sunburns both rise in summer.

vocab.def: The part of a map that explains what its symbols, colors, or labels mean.
vocab.example: A star in the key stands for the county seat.

vocab.def: The part of a map that shows how distance on the map compares to real distance.
A symbol on a map that shows the directions north, south, east, and west.
vocab.example: The compass rose shows that north is at the top of the map.

vocab.def: A judgment reached by reasoning from evidence; on the GED it must be supported by the information given.
vocab.example: The table shows the population roughly doubled from 1900 to 1950.

vocab.def: Words chosen to stir strong positive or negative feelings.
vocab.example: Calling protesters “a mob” instead of “a crowd.”

stimuli.title: Political Cartoon: “Join, or Die” (1754)
stimuli.html:
Description of the cartoon: A snake is drawn cut into eight separate pieces lying in a line. Each piece is labeled with initials standing for a British colony or region in North America; from the tail to the head they read S.C., N.C., V., M., P., N.J., N.Y., and N.E. (New England). Below the snake are the words “JOIN, or DIE.”

Background: Benjamin Franklin published the cartoon in his newspaper, the Pennsylvania Gazette, in May 1754. At the time, Britain and France were competing for control of North America, and fighting had begun on the frontier in what became the French and Indian War. A popular belief of the time held that a snake cut into pieces could come back to life if the pieces were joined before sunset.

stimuli.title: World War I Recruiting Poster (1917)
stimuli.html:
Description of the poster: Uncle Sam, a figure who stands for the United States, is shown from the chest up. He has white hair and a white beard and wears a tall hat decorated with white stars on a blue band. He stares directly at the viewer, frowning slightly, and points his finger straight out of the poster. Large letters read “I WANT YOU FOR U.S. ARMY.” Smaller letters underneath say “NEAREST RECRUITING STATION.”

Background: The artist James Montgomery Flagg created the poster. The United States entered World War I in April 1917, and more than four million copies of the poster were printed in 1917 and 1918.

stimuli.title: Two Sources on the Banking Crisis of 1933
stimuli.html:
Source A

This great Nation will endure as it has endured, will revive and will prosper. So, first of all, let me assert my firm belief that the only thing we have to fear is fear itself—nameless, unreasoning, unjustified terror which paralyzes needed efforts to convert retreat into advance. …

Values have shrunken to fantastic levels; taxes have risen; our ability to pay has fallen; government of all kinds is faced by serious curtailment of income; the means of exchange are frozen in the currents of trade; the withered leaves of industrial enterprise lie on every side; farmers find no markets for their produce; the savings of many years in thousands of families are gone. More important, a host of unemployed citizens face the grim problem of existence, and an equally great number toil with little return.

—President Franklin D. Roosevelt, First Inaugural Address, March 4, 1933

Source B

When Franklin D. Roosevelt took office on March 4, 1933, the nation was in the fourth year of the Great Depression. About one in four workers was unemployed, and thousands of banks had failed since the stock market crash of October 1929. Frightened depositors were rushing to withdraw their savings, which pushed still more banks toward collapse. Two days after his inauguration, Roosevelt declared a national bank holiday that closed the nation's banks. Congress quickly passed the Emergency Banking Act, and banks that inspectors judged to be sound began to reopen within days. Historians generally credit Roosevelt's calm, confident speeches with helping to restore public trust in the banks.

—From a U.S. history textbook chapter written for this course
stimuli.source: Source A: public-domain presidential address. Source B: original text.

stimuli.title: The Dust Bowl
stimuli.html:
During World War I (1914–1918), wheat prices were high, and new gasoline-powered tractors made it possible to plow land faster than ever. Farmers on the southern Great Plains plowed up millions of acres of native grasses, whose deep roots had held the soil in place, and planted wheat.

In the early 1930s, a long drought began. Crops died, and the bare, dry soil was exposed to the strong Plains winds. Huge dust storms followed. In May 1934, one storm carried dust all the way to Washington, D.C., and out over the Atlantic Ocean. On April 14, 1935, a day remembered as “Black Sunday,” a massive storm turned the sky dark across the region.

Many farm families lost their crops and could not pay their debts. Thousands left the Plains, many heading west to California to look for work. In April 1935, Congress passed the Soil Conservation Act, which created the Soil Conservation Service to teach farmers methods, such as planting trees as windbreaks and plowing along the natural curves of the land, that would help keep soil from blowing away.

stimuli.title: Two Accounts of a Strike (fictional)
stimuli.html:
The two accounts below were written for this lesson. They describe the same fictional event: a strike at the Harmon Textile Mill in 1911.

Account 1: Statement by mill owner Charles Harmon, printed in the company newsletter
The Harmon Mill has always paid fair wages, and our workers have been loyal for twenty years. This trouble was stirred up by outside agitators who misled good people with false promises. When business slowed this spring, we made a small, necessary adjustment to wages so that the mill could stay open and keep every worker employed. The mill will reopen Monday for all loyal employees who wish to return.

Account 2: Letter from mill worker Rose Kowalski to her sister
We walked out on Tuesday, more than three hundred of us. In April the company cut our pay by one tenth, but we still work fifty-six hours a week, and rent did not go down. No one from outside told us to strike. We voted ourselves, in the church hall. Mr. Harmon says we are disloyal, but all we ask is the pay we had before.

items.prompt: In which direction is the town of Ridgeway from the town of Carver?
options: Northeast
Southwest
Northwest
Southeast
items.hint: Start at Carver (E2). Which way do you travel to reach Ridgeway (C4)? Check rows first, then columns.
items.explain:
Step 1: Carver is in square E2 and Ridgeway is in square C4.
Step 2: Rows: going from row E to row C means moving up the map, which is north.
Step 3: Columns: going from column 2 to column 4 means moving right, which is east.
Step 4: North + east = northeast.

“Southwest” is the direction of Carver from Ridgeway, the reverse of what the question asks.

items.prompt: Using the map, about how many miles is it from Millford to Eastport, measured in a straight line from the center of one square to the center of the other?
items.hint: Both towns are in row B. Count how many squares apart they are, then use the scale.
items.explain:
Step 1: Millford is in B2 and Eastport is in B5, both in row B.
Step 2: From column 2 to column 5 is 5 − 2 = 3 squares.
Step 3: Each square is 5 miles: 3 × 5 = 15 miles.

A common error is counting the squares B2, B3, B4, and B5 as 4 squares (20 miles). Center to center, the distance is the number of squares you move, which is 3.

items.prompt: Drag each source into the correct category.
choices: A letter a Union soldier wrote to his family in 1863
A high school textbook chapter on the Civil War published in 2019
A photograph taken at a civil rights march in 1963
A documentary film about the Great Depression made in 2010, featuring interviews with historians
The text of the Nineteenth Amendment as ratified in 1920
An encyclopedia article summarizing the causes of World War I
items.hint: Ask: Was this made by someone who was there, at the time? Or was it made later to explain the past?
items.explain:
Primary sources were created at the time by participants or witnesses: the soldier's 1863 letter, the 1963 photograph taken at the march, and the Nineteenth Amendment itself (an original government document from 1920).

Secondary sources were created later to explain or interpret the past: the 2019 textbook, the 2010 documentary, and the encyclopedia article.

The documentary is a common trap. Even if it shows old film clips, the documentary as a whole was made decades later and presents historians' interpretations, so it is secondary.

items.prompt: Which method of getting to work showed the largest increase in percent of workers from 2005 to 2025?
options: Worked from home
Public transit
Drove alone
Walked or biked
items.hint: For each method, subtract the 2005 value from the 2025 value.
items.explain:
Change from 2005 to 2025 for each method:
Drove alone: 58 − 68 = −10
Carpooled: 8 − 12 = −4
Public transit: 13 − 11 = +2
Walked or biked: 6 − 5 = +1
Worked from home: 15 − 4 = +11

Worked from home increased the most. “Drove alone” had the largest change, but it was a decrease, not an increase. Public transit rose, but by only 2 percentage points.

items.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the graph?
options: A smaller share of workers drove alone in 2025 than in 2005, but driving alone was still the most common method in 2025.
The number of workers who used public transit doubled between 2005 and 2025.
Fewer people worked in Carver City in 2025 than in 2005.
The light-rail line caused more workers to work from home.
items.hint: The graph shows percents, not numbers of people, and it does not explain why anything changed.
items.explain:
Driving alone fell from 68% to 58%, so a smaller share drove alone. In 2025, 58% is still higher than every other method (8%, 13%, 6%, 15%), so it remained the most common. Both parts of the statement are shown on the graph.

The transit choice is wrong for two reasons: 11% to 13% is not a doubling, and percents do not tell you the number of riders. The graph gives no total number of workers, so it cannot show whether fewer people worked in the city. Nothing on the graph shows that the rail line caused any change; the graph shows only what changed, not why, and it does not connect the rail line to working from home at all.

items.prompt: The sentences below are from a draft of a local news article. A news article should report facts. Click the sentence that states an opinion rather than a fact.
spans: The Ridgeway Public Library will extend its weekday hours beginning March 1.
Under the new schedule, the library will close at 9 p.m. instead of 6 p.m. Monday through Thursday.
The change will cost about $42,000 per year, according to the county budget office.
The county board approved the plan by a vote of 4 to 1 on Tuesday.
Keeping the doors open later is the smartest investment the county has made in years.
Library staff said the new hours will be covered by hiring two part-time workers.
items.hint: Look for a sentence with a judgment word that people could reasonably disagree about.
items.explain:
“Keeping the doors open later is the smartest investment the county has made in years” is an opinion. “Smartest investment” is a judgment, and there is no way to prove it true or false.

Every other sentence can be checked: the start date, the new closing time, the cost reported by the budget office, the 4-to-1 vote, and what the staff said. The sentence about cost contains a number, but numbers do not make a sentence a fact or an opinion; what matters is whether it can be verified.

items.prompt: What was Benjamin Franklin's main message in the 1754 cartoon?
options: The colonies needed to unite in order to survive the threat they faced.
The colonies should declare independence from Great Britain.
New England was stronger than the other colonies and should lead them.
Snakes were a serious danger to settlers on the frontier.
items.hint: Think about the popular belief described in the background, and the words printed under the snake.
items.explain:
The snake is cut into separate pieces, one for each colony or region. The caption says “JOIN, or DIE,” and the background explains the belief that a cut snake could live again only if its pieces were joined. Franklin's message: the colonies must unite or be defeated one by one during the conflict with France.

The independence choice is a common mistake. The cartoon was later reused during the American Revolution, but in 1754 the colonies were fighting alongside Britain against France, and nothing in the cartoon calls for breaking away from Britain. New England is just one segment; the cartoon does not rank the colonies. The snake is a symbol, not a warning about real snakes.

items.prompt:
Complete the statements about the poster.

The poster uses Uncle Sam, a well-known symbol of the United States, so that viewers connect the feelings they have about their country with joining the army. This propaganda technique is called {{0}}. The main purpose of the poster was to {{1}}. Because it was created to persuade, the poster is most useful to a historian as evidence of {{2}}.

options: transfer
bandwagon
testimonial
card stacking
persuade men to enlist in the U.S. Army
report how many soldiers were already serving
explain why the United States entered the war
ask citizens to grow more food
how the government tried to build public support for the war
the exact number of men who enlisted because of the poster
how every American felt about the war in 1917
the battles the U.S. Army fought in Europe

items.hint: Which technique links an idea to a respected symbol? Then read the words printed on the poster.
items.explain:
Blank 1: transfer. Transfer links a cause to a respected symbol (here, Uncle Sam) so the viewer's feelings for the symbol carry over to the cause. Bandwagon would say “everyone is joining”; testimonial would use a real famous person's endorsement; card stacking would present a one-sided list of facts. None of these appear in the description.

Blank 2: persuade men to enlist. The words “I WANT YOU FOR U.S. ARMY” and “NEAREST RECRUITING STATION” tell viewers to sign up. The poster gives no numbers and no reasons for the war, and it says nothing about food.

Blank 3: how the government tried to build support. A persuasive poster shows what its makers wanted people to think and do. It cannot show how many men actually enlisted because of it or how all Americans felt.

items.prompt: Which statement best explains why Source A is a primary source and Source B is a secondary source?
options: Source A was created by a participant at the time of the events, while Source B was written later by someone describing and interpreting those events.
Source A is more accurate than Source B because it comes from the president.
Source A expresses opinions, while Source B contains only facts.
Source A is about the whole economy, while Source B is only about banks.
items.hint: The difference between primary and secondary sources is about who created the source and when, not about accuracy.
items.explain:
Source A is President Roosevelt's own speech, given on March 4, 1933, as the crisis was happening, so it is a primary source. Source B is a textbook passage written long afterward that explains the events and includes historians' judgments, so it is a secondary source.

Primary sources are not automatically more accurate; a speech is meant to persuade and shows one person's view. Source B is not purely factual either: its last sentence reports an interpretation (“Historians generally credit…”). Topic does not determine source type.

items.prompt: Which pieces of information appear in Source B but not in Source A? Select two answers.
options: About how large a share of workers was unemployed
That Roosevelt declared a national bank holiday that closed the nation's banks
That many families had lost their savings
That farmers could not find markets for their crops
That Roosevelt believed fear itself was a danger to recovery
items.hint: For each choice, check Source A first. If you can find it there, it is not a correct answer.
items.explain:
Correct: Source B says “About one in four workers was unemployed.” Source A mentions “a host of unemployed citizens” but never gives a share or number. Source B also describes the national bank holiday, which happened two days after the speech, so Source A could not include it.

Incorrect: Lost savings (“the savings of many years in thousands of families are gone”), farmers without markets (“farmers find no markets for their produce”), and fear as a danger (“the only thing we have to fear is fear itself”) all appear in Source A.

items.prompt: Which sequence of events correctly shows the chain of causes and effects described in the passage?
options: High wheat prices → native grasses plowed up → drought leaves soil bare and dry → wind carries soil away in dust storms
Dust storms → native grasses plowed up → high wheat prices → drought begins
Soil Conservation Service created → drought begins → farmers plow native grasses → dust storms
Families move to California → farms are abandoned → wheat prices rise → dust storms
items.hint: Find the earliest event in the passage and follow the words that show what each event led to.
items.explain:
Step 1: High wheat prices during World War I encouraged farmers to plow up native grasses.
Step 2: The grasses' deep roots had held the soil; without them, the soil was unprotected.
Step 3: The drought of the early 1930s killed crops and left the bare soil dry.
Step 4: Strong winds carried the soil away in dust storms.

The other sequences put effects before causes. The Soil Conservation Service was created in 1935 as a response to the dust storms, and families moved to California as an effect of the disaster, not as a cause of it.

items.prompt: Which statement best explains why the two accounts describe the strike so differently?
options: Each writer's position in the conflict shapes which facts he or she includes and the words used to describe the strike.
Account 1 is a primary source, while Account 2 is a secondary source written years later.
The two writers are describing two different strikes that happened at the mill.
Account 2 was written to be published in a newspaper, while Account 1 was private.
items.hint: Who wrote each account, and what does each writer want the reader to believe?
items.explain:
Both accounts describe the same 1911 strike, and both are primary sources written at the time. They differ because of point of view. The owner calls the pay cut a “small, necessary adjustment,” blames “outside agitators” (name-calling), and calls returning workers “loyal.” The worker gives specific details the owner leaves out (a one-tenth pay cut, fifty-six-hour weeks, rent that did not go down) and says the workers voted to strike themselves.

Account 2 is a private letter to a sister, and Account 1 was printed in the company newsletter, so the last choice reverses the facts. Account 2 is not a later secondary source; it was written by a participant during the strike.
